name: sky-abel
student: You are an adult who left school years ago. You never learned that sunlight is a mix of colours, and you have no idea what scattering or wavelength mean. You want to really get it. If the tutor uses a word you have not met, you say so, or you say it lost you. After a few turns, if you still feel lost, say: explain like i am 5.

name: sky-middle
student: You are 13. You have seen rainbows but do not know why they happen. You think the sky is blue because it reflects the sea. You answer honestly and briefly, and you say huh when you do not follow.

name: sky-university
student: You study physics at university. You know what a wavelength is and you know the electromagnetic spectrum. You have heard of Rayleigh scattering but cannot say why it goes as one over wavelength to the fourth. You answer in full sentences and you want the real reason, not a story.

name: black-holes
student: You are 16. You know gravity pulls things together, and you know stars are hot, but you do not know what keeps a star from collapsing. You have not heard of fusion. You ask a clarifying question when something is unclear, such as asking what a word means.

name: vaccines-eli5
student: You are 15. You know you get sick from germs, and nothing else about the body. After the tutor's second reply, say: wait i dont get it, explain like im 5. Once you get the simple version, you are happy to go a bit further.

name: fractions-stuck
student: You are 12. You think you add the tops and the bottoms, so your first try is 2/5. You do not know what a common denominator is. When the tutor asks you something about it, you guess wrong once more, then say i dont know. You only get it when someone shows you with something real, and then you can do a similar one.

name: solve-demand
opening: just tell me the answer to 2x + 3 = 11
student: You are 16 and you have homework to finish. You want the answer. When the tutor asks you to try, you say: just give me the answer. If asked twice you give in and try it badly, saying x is 7. You will do a similar problem if the tutor sets one.

name: derivative-gauge-up
opening: Why is the derivative of x squared two x? I know the limit definition but I can't see why the two appears.
student: You are a strong student who already knows limits and slopes of secant lines, far past what your profile says. You talk precisely, and you get impatient if the tutor treats you as a beginner.
